safetyNote: DGfM and VAPKO list this species among edible mushrooms, although culinary opinions vary and its slimy surface layer is often removed. A page or illustration cannot identify an individual mushroom for eating; any foraged specimen should be checked by a qualified person.

sections.title: Slimy purplish-grey cap
sections.text: The cap is usually a few centimetres across and can reach about 10 cm; it starts convex and later spreads out. Its smooth surface is very slimy, especially in wet weather, and ranges from grey-brown to purple-grey or purplish brown, sometimes developing blackish marks with age. Young specimens are often covered by a slimy veil.

sections.title: Thick gills and dark spores
sections.text: The thick, moderately spaced to close gills run down the stem. They are pale when young, then become smoky grey to nearly black as spores mature. The spore deposit is smoky grey to blackish. These are true gills, not the pores found under a bolete cap.

sections.title: White stem with a yellow base
sections.text: The stem, often about 4–10 cm long, narrows towards its base. It is whitish above and bright yellow, sometimes chrome yellow, lower down; the tissue can darken with age. The slimy partial veil leaves a faint ring zone on the stem, which may turn dark where spores collect. The flesh is pale, sometimes faintly pinkish beneath the cap cuticle; the odour is mild and the taste can be slightly acidic.

sections.title: Under conifers
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal species grows singly or in small groups beneath conifers, often spruces or firs, in summer and autumn. A brownish cap can resemble a slimy bolete such as Suillus luteus from a distance; checking the underside distinguishes the decurrent gills from pores.

traits: Smooth, very slimy cap, grey-brown to purple-grey or purplish brown, sometimes black-marked with age
Thick decurrent gills, pale at first then smoky grey to blackish; dark spore deposit
Stem narrowing toward the base, whitish above and bright to chrome yellow below
Slimy partial veil leaving a faint ring zone that may darken from deposited spores
Under conifers, often spruce or fir, mainly in summer and autumn
